mainTopic: Dew, wind, clouds and rain: which are never withheld, how this shapes mistakes in משיב הרוח ומוריד הגשם, and the value of different kinds of weather
overview: The גמרא finishes explaining that טל (dew) is never held back. It then answers why אליהו swore there would be no dew: he meant the special טל של ברכה. Next, רבי יהושע בן לוי proves from a פסוק in זכריה that רוחות (winds) never stop, since the world cannot exist without them, just as it cannot exist without ישראל. רבי חנינא draws practical הלכה from this: a mistake about wind or dew in the second ברכה of שמונה עשרה never requires repeating, but a mistake about rain does. A ברייתא says mentioning clouds and winds is optional, and the גמרא resolves a contradiction from רב יוסף by separating early clouds from late clouds and ordinary winds from unusual winds. The גמרא then discusses how helpful clouds, wind and sun are after rain, and when wind after rain becomes a curse instead. Finally, רבא teaches that snow on the mountains is worth five rainfalls and begins listing which kind of rain helps what. That list continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Dew is never held back
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes its answer: dew does not need to be mentioned or restored because it is never withheld.
steps.simpleTranslation: ...because it [dew] is not held back.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the end of a sentence from the previous section. It explains why the פסוק about ending the drought mentions only rain returning and not dew: dew never stopped.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, the גמרא noted that אליהו swore there would be no טל and no מטר. But when the drought ended, only rain was promised back. The answer is that טל is always present, so it never needed to come back.

phrases.english: because it is not withheld.
phrases.notes: Completes the answer begun on the previous amud (מאי טעמא? משום...).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the answer earlier about why dew was not restored.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Dew was not restored because it never stops.
steps.whyThisMatters: The idea that טל never stops is the foundation for רבי חנינא's הלכה here.

steps.title: Then why did אליהו swear about dew?
steps.stepSummary: If dew never stops, אליהו's oath that there would be no dew seems pointless.
steps.simpleTranslation: And since dew is never withheld, why did אליהו need to swear about it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer it just gave. If dew always comes, אליהו's oath 'there will be no dew' makes no sense.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אליהו said, 'there will be neither טל nor מטר' (מלכים א יז:א). A נביא would not swear about something that cannot happen. So the claim that dew is never withheld seems to clash with the פסוק.

phrases.english: But since it is not withheld,
why did Elijah need to swear?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer in step 1.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that dew is never withheld.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: אליהו swore that dew would stop. That implies dew can be withheld.

steps.title: אליהו meant the special dew of blessing
steps.stepSummary: אליהו's oath was about טל של ברכה, the helpful dew, not ordinary dew.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what he told him: even the dew of blessing will not come.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that אליהו was not talking about ordinary dew. He meant that even the extra, blessed dew that helps crops grow would stop.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two kinds of dew. Ordinary dew never stops. טל של ברכה, the beneficial kind, can be withheld. אליהו's oath referred only to the second kind.

keyTerms.meaning: Dew of blessing, the beneficial dew that helps crops

phrases.english: This is what he said to him:

phrases.aramaic: אֲפִילּוּ טַל בְּרָכָה נָמֵי לָא אָתֵי.
phrases.english: even the dew of blessing will also not come.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 2.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpretation, by splitting dew into two categories
steps.terutzHavaAmina: אליהו meant that all dew would stop.
steps.terutzMaskana: He meant only טל של ברכה. Ordinary dew continued.

steps.title: Then the פסוק should restore the dew of blessing
steps.stepSummary: If טל של ברכה was withheld, the פסוק ending the drought should have promised it back.
steps.simpleTranslation: Then let Him bring back the dew of blessing!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes further. If the blessed dew really stopped, then when the drought ended, the פסוק should have said it was coming back too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer in step 3 creates a new problem. Now something really was withheld, yet the פסוק 'ואתנה מטר' mentions only rain returning. So the גמרא asks why the blessed dew is not mentioned.

phrases.english: But let Him restore the dew of blessing!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in step 3.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that the oath was about טל של ברכה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the blessed dew was withheld, its return should have been announced along with the rain.

steps.title: The return of blessed dew is not noticeable
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק did not mention it because people cannot tell the blessed dew apart from regular dew.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because the matter is not noticeable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that there was no point in announcing the return of the blessed dew. People cannot see the difference between it and ordinary dew.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Rain returning is obvious to everyone, so it was announced. Blessed dew looks the same as regular dew, so announcing it would not show anything clear. This ends the discussion about dew.
steps.whatToRemember: Ordinary טל never stops. Only טל של ברכה can be withheld, and its return is not noticeable.

phrases.english: Because the matter is not recognizable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 4 and closes the discussion about dew.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Practical explanation of why the פסוק is silent
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוק should have announced the return of the blessed dew.
steps.terutzMaskana: There was no need, since its return cannot be noticed.

steps.title: Where do we learn that winds never stop?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא moves from dew to winds and asks for a source that רוחות are never withheld.
steps.simpleTranslation: But winds, from where do we know that they are not withheld?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא switches topics from dew to wind. It asks for a source that winds always blow. This sets up the next step, which brings a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier ברייתא said that both טל and רוחות do not need to be mentioned. Dew now has a source in the אליהו story. Wind still needs its own proof.

phrases.english: But winds, from where do we know
that they are not withheld?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns from dew, now settled, to wind.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A scriptural source that winds are never withheld.

steps.title: רבי יהושע בן לוי brings a פסוק about the four winds
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע בן לוי cites זכריה: 'like the four winds of the heavens I have spread you.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהושע בן לוי said: the פסוק says, 'For like the four winds of the heavens I have spread you out, says ה׳.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע בן לוי offers a פסוק as the source for the idea that winds never stop.
steps.deeperAnalysis: At first glance, the פסוק does not clearly say anything about winds never stopping. The next steps will work out how the פסוק teaches this.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said,
for the verse says:
"For like the four winds of the heavens
I have spread you out, says the Lord."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי, דְּאָמַר קְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 6 with a פסוק.

steps.title: What does the פסוק mean? A first suggestion
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the פסוק means and suggests it is about scattering ישראל to the four directions.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is He telling them? If you say the הקדוש ברוך הוא is telling ישראל: 'I scattered you to the four winds of the world'...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks how this פסוק proves anything about wind. It tries a first, simple reading: it describes the exile across the four directions. This reading is about to be tested.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the פסוק only describes exile, it says nothing about winds never stopping, and the proof fails. 'אילימא' signals that this reading is a suggestion the גמרא will reject.

keyTerms.meaning: If you say (introduces a reading about to be rejected)

phrases.english: What is He saying to them?
If you say this is what He says to them —
the Holy One, Blessed be He, to Israel:
that I scattered you to the four directions of the world,

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי קָאָמַר לְהוּ? אִילֵּימָא הָכִי קָאָמַר לְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Examines the meaning of the פסוק cited in step 7.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the פסוק means, and how it proves that winds never stop.

steps.title: The word 'like' rules out the simple reading
steps.stepSummary: If the פסוק meant scattering, it would say 'בארבע' (to the four), not 'כארבע' (like the four).
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, why 'like the four'? It should have said 'to the four'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the first reading because of one letter. The פסוק says 'כ' (like), not 'ב' (to/in).
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Scattered to the four winds' would need 'בארבע'. The word 'כארבע' signals a comparison: ישראל is like the winds in some way. So the פסוק is comparing, not describing a location.

keyTerms.meaning: Like the four / to the four

phrases.english: If so — why "like the four"?
It should have said "to the four"!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the reading proposed in step 8.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The prefix כ means 'like', which does not fit a description of location.
steps.confusionAlert: The whole argument turns on one letter: כ (like) versus ב (to/in). Read the two words carefully.

steps.title: The world cannot exist without wind, nor without ישראל
steps.stepSummary: The correct reading: just as the world cannot exist without winds, it cannot exist without ישראל.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, this is what He means: just as the world cannot be without winds, so the world cannot be without ישראל.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the correct meaning of the פסוק. It is a comparison: ישראל is as essential to the world as the winds are.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The comparison only works if winds truly never stop and the world always needs them. So the פסוק assumes winds are never withheld, which proves the point from step 6.
steps.whatToRemember: The proof that wind never stops: 'כארבע רוחות' compares ישראל to wind. Both are things the world cannot exist without.

phrases.english: Rather, this is what He is saying:

phrases.aramaic: כְּשֵׁם שֶׁאִי אֶפְשָׁר לָעוֹלָם בְּלֹא רוּחוֹת —
phrases.english: just as the world cannot exist without winds —

phrases.aramaic: כָּךְ אִי אֶפְשָׁר לָעוֹלָם בְּלֹא יִשְׂרָאֵל.
phrases.english: so too the world cannot exist without Israel.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the rejected reading with the correct one, completing the proof.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוק compares ישראל to the winds, which assumes that winds never stop.

steps.title: רבי חנינא's rule for the summer
steps.stepSummary: In summer, saying 'משיב הרוח' by mistake does not require repeating. Saying 'מוריד הגשם' does.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חנינא said: Therefore, in the summer, if one said 'He makes the wind blow,' we do not make him go back. If he said 'He makes the rain fall,' we make him go back.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חנינא draws a practical הלכה from what was just proven. He starts with mistakes made during the summer in the שמונה עשרה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'הלכך' (therefore) ties this ruling to the idea that wind always blows. Praising ה׳ for wind in summer is still true, so no harm is done. Praising ה׳ as 'מוריד הגשם' in summer is wrong, since summer rain is a curse, so he must repeat.

keyTerms.meaning: We make him go back and repeat

phrases.english: Rabbi Ḥanina said: Therefore,
in the summer days:
if one said "He makes the wind blow" —
we do not make him go back.
if one said "He makes the rain fall" —
we make him go back.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the principle that wind and dew never stop to practical תפילה law.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In summer, mentioning wind by mistake needs no repetition. Mentioning rain requires repetition.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is practical הלכה for anyone who makes a mistake in the second ברכה of שמונה עשרה.

steps.title: רבי חנינא's rule for the rainy season
steps.stepSummary: In winter, leaving out 'משיב הרוח' does not require repeating. Leaving out 'מוריד הגשם' does.
steps.simpleTranslation: In the rainy season, if he did not say 'He makes the wind blow,' we do not make him go back. If he did not say 'He makes the rain fall,' we make him go back.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חנינא continues with the opposite season. Now the mistake is leaving something out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Wind comes anyway, so leaving it out does no harm. Rain is the needed blessing of winter, so leaving it out is a real omission and he must repeat.

phrases.english: In the rainy season:
if one did not say "He makes the wind blow" —
we do not make him go back.
if one did not say "He makes the rain fall" —
we make him go back.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Mirrors step 11 for the winter season.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In winter, leaving out wind needs no repetition. Leaving out rain requires repetition.

steps.title: Even saying the opposite about wind and dew is not a problem
steps.stepSummary: Even if he said 'מעביר הרוח ומפריח הטל' (He removes the wind and blows away the dew), he does not repeat.
steps.simpleTranslation: And not only that, but even if he said 'He removes the wind and blows away the dew,' we do not make him go back.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חנינא adds a bigger case. Even a wrong statement about wind and dew does not require repeating.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since wind and dew never stop, his mistaken words have no real effect. His words cannot cancel what ה׳ always provides. This is the strongest application of the principle.

keyTerms.meaning: And not only that, but even

steps.whatToRemember: Because טל and רוחות never stop, mistakes about them in שמונה עשרה never require repeating. Only mistakes about גשם do.

phrases.english: And not only that, but even if he said
"He removes the wind and blows away the dew" —
we do not make him go back.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends step 12 to an even more extreme case.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: No mistake about wind or dew, even saying the opposite, requires repeating the ברכה, because they never stop.

steps.title: A ברייתא says mentioning clouds and winds is optional
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא rules that חכמים did not require mentioning clouds and winds in תפילה, but a person may mention them if he wants.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: חכמים did not require people to mention clouds and winds. But if someone wants to mention them, he may.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that fits the previous ruling: you do not have to go back if you left out 'משיב הרוח'. Mentioning wind and clouds is optional.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This explains why leaving out 'משיב הרוח' does not require repeating the תפילה. Wind, like clouds, was never made a required mention. Mentioning it is allowed but not required.

phrases.english: It was taught: regarding clouds and regarding winds,
the Sages did not require one to mention them,
but if he wishes to mention them, he may mention them.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנָא: בֶּעָבִים וּבָרוּחוֹת לֹא חִיְּיבוּ חֲכָמִים לְהַזְכִּיר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the earlier rulings that leaving out or changing the wind phrase does not require repeating the תפילה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Mentioning clouds and winds is optional, not required.

steps.title: Why is mentioning them optional?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the reason behind the ברייתא's ruling.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why clouds and winds do not need to be mentioned. It is setting up the explanation that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a real question asking for information, not an attack. The ברייתא gave a ruling without a reason, so the גמרא wants to know the logic.

phrases.english: What is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reasoning behind the ברייתא in step 14.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why are clouds and winds left out of the required mentions?

steps.title: Because clouds and winds are never held back
steps.stepSummary: Clouds and winds never stop, so there is no need to ask for them.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because they are not held back.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that clouds and winds are always around and are never withheld. So there is no need to pray for them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We mention rain because God may hold it back as a punishment, so it depends on our תפילה. Clouds and winds come regardless, according to this answer. That is why mentioning them is only optional.

phrases.english: Because they are not withheld.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 15.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Clouds and winds are never withheld, so there is no need to pray for them.

steps.title: Challenge: רב יוסף teaches that God does withhold clouds and winds
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף's ברייתא reads 'וְעָצַר אֶת הַשָּׁמַיִם' as God withholding clouds and winds. The same פסוק already mentions rain separately, so this phrase must mean something else.
steps.simpleTranslation: Are they really never held back? But רב יוסף taught: 'And He will close up the heavens' means from clouds and winds. You might ask whether it only means rain. But the פסוק already says 'there will be no rain,' so rain is already covered. So what does 'close up the heavens' mean? It means clouds and winds.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the reason just given. It quotes a ברייתא showing that God can hold back clouds and winds as a punishment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יוסף shows that 'וְעָצַר אֶת הַשָּׁמַיִם' cannot be about rain, because the end of the פסוק mentions rain on its own. So the phrase must teach that clouds and winds can be withheld. That directly contradicts the claim 'דְּלָא מִיעַצְרִי'.

keyTerms.meaning: But didn't [he] teach? (introduces a contradicting ברייתא)
And He will close up the heavens
So how do I explain [this phrase]?

phrases.english: And are they not withheld?
But didn't Rav Yosef teach:
"And He will close up the heavens" —
from the clouds and from the winds.

phrases.aramaic: אַתָּה אוֹמֵר מִן הֶעָבִים וּמִן הָרוּחוֹת,
phrases.english: Do you say it means from the clouds and from the winds,
or perhaps it refers only to rain?
When it says, "And there will be no rain" —
rain is already mentioned.

phrases.aramaic: הָא מָה אֲנִי מְקַיֵּים ״וְעָצַר אֶת הַשָּׁמַיִם״ —
phrases.english: So how do I explain "And He will close up the heavens"?
It means from the clouds and from the winds.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reason given in step 16.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that clouds and winds are never withheld.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב יוסף's ברייתא reads the פסוק as saying God does withhold clouds and winds as a punishment. If so, they are things we would need to pray for.

steps.title: The two contradictions stated clearly
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא sums up the problem. The two ברייתות contradict each other about winds, and also about clouds.
steps.simpleTranslation: The statement about winds contradicts the other statement about winds. The statement about clouds contradicts the other statement about clouds!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא clearly names the two contradictions it must now solve, one about winds and one about clouds. This sets up the two answers that follow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By splitting the problem in two, the גמרא shows that winds and clouds may need different solutions. Each will be handled separately.

phrases.english: Winds against winds is difficult,
clouds against clouds is difficult!

steps.triggerLanguage: קַשְׁיָא רוּחוֹת אַרוּחוֹת, קַשְׁיָא עָבִים אַעָבִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: States the contradiction raised in step 17 as two separate problems.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: One ברייתא says clouds and winds are never withheld. The other says they can be withheld.

steps.title: Clouds: early clouds versus late clouds
steps.stepSummary: The first ברייתא is about early clouds, which always come. רב יוסף's ברייתא is about late clouds, which can be withheld.
steps.simpleTranslation: The clouds contradiction is not difficult. This one is about early clouds, and that one is about late clouds.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא solves the clouds contradiction. It explains that each ברייתא is talking about a different kind of cloud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Early clouds come before the rain and appear whether or not rain falls, so they are never withheld. Late clouds come after the rain, and God can hold them back as a punishment. So 'clouds' is one category, but the two kinds behave differently.

keyTerms.meaning: This one... that one... (splits two sources into different cases)

phrases.english: Clouds against clouds is not difficult:
this one refers to early clouds,
that one refers to late clouds.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the clouds half of step 18.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases: each source speaks about a different type of cloud.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both ברייתות seemed to be about the same clouds.
steps.terutzMaskana: Early clouds are never withheld (first ברייתא). Late clouds can be withheld (רב יוסף).

steps.title: Winds: ordinary winds versus unusual winds
steps.stepSummary: The first ברייתא is about ordinary winds, which always blow. רב יוסף's ברייתא is about unusual winds, which can be withheld.
steps.simpleTranslation: The winds contradiction is not difficult. This one is about a common wind, and that one is about an uncommon wind.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא solves the winds contradiction in the same way. Each ברייתא is talking about a different kind of wind.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Ordinary winds are always present and never withheld, so we need not mention them. Unusual, stronger winds can be held back, and that is what רב יוסף's ברייתא means.

phrases.english: Winds against winds is not difficult:
this one refers to a common wind,
that one refers to an uncommon wind.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the winds half of step 18.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases: each source speaks about a different type of wind.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both ברייתות seemed to be about the same winds.
steps.terutzMaskana: Common winds are never withheld. Uncommon winds can be withheld.

steps.title: But unusual winds are needed for threshing
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that unusual winds are useful for winnowing grain, so we should have to pray for them.
steps.simpleTranslation: But an uncommon wind is useful for the threshing floor!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer about winds. If unusual winds can be withheld and people need them, why are we not required to pray for them?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Farmers used strong winds to blow the chaff away from the grain on the threshing floor. Since these winds can be withheld and are useful, it seems they should be included in our required mention.

phrases.english: An uncommon wind
is useful for the threshing floor!

steps.triggerLanguage: רוּחַ שֶׁאֵינָהּ מְצוּיָה חַזְיָא לְבֵי דָרֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the winds answer in step 20.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that unusual winds need not be prayed for.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Unusual winds can be withheld and are needed for winnowing, so we should be required to pray for them.

steps.title: Grain can be winnowed with sieves instead
steps.stepSummary: Unusual winds are not truly needed, because grain can be cleaned with sieves.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is possible to do it with sieves.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that people can clean grain with sieves when there is no wind. So these winds are not essential, and we need not pray for them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We are required to pray only for things we truly depend on, like rain. Since there is another way to winnow, unusual wind is a convenience, not a necessity. This keeps the ruling that mentioning wind is optional.
steps.whatToRemember: Mentioning clouds and winds is optional. Early clouds and ordinary winds are never withheld. Late clouds and unusual winds can be withheld. Unusual winds are not essential, since grain can be winnowed with sieves.

phrases.english: It is possible with sieves.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 21.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Minimizing the need: there is another way to get the same result.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Unusual winds are a real need, so we should have to pray for them.
steps.terutzMaskana: Sieves can do the job, so unusual winds are not a necessity and need not be mentioned.

steps.title: Clouds and winds are second only to rain
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that clouds and winds are next in importance after rain.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: Clouds and winds are second to rain.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא that praises clouds and winds as almost as helpful as rain itself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Up to now the topic was whether clouds and winds can be withheld. Now a new teaching says how valuable they are: just one level below rain. It does not yet say which clouds and winds it means, and that is the next question.

keyTerms.meaning: Second to rain, next in benefit after rain

phrases.english: It was taught:
Clouds and winds
are second to rain.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the theme of clouds and winds from steps 18-22, but turns to their value.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Clouds and winds are second in benefit only to rain.

steps.title: Which clouds and winds are meant?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks in what situation clouds and winds are so helpful.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a short clarifying question to set up the next step: when exactly are clouds and winds this helpful?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Not every cloud or wind is good, so the ברייתא needs a definition. This question opens the door for עולא's answer.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? How do we picture it?

phrases.english: What is the case?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the exact case of the ברייתא in step 23.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: In what circumstances are clouds and winds second to rain?

steps.title: Clouds and winds that come after rain
steps.stepSummary: עולא (or רב יהודה) says the ברייתא means clouds and winds that come after rain.
steps.simpleTranslation: עולא said, and some say רב יהודה: Those that come after rain.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question: the helpful clouds and winds are the ones that come right after it rains.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא is now limited to a specific time: after rainfall. The name of the speaker is uncertain, so the גמרא gives both possibilities, עולא or רב יהודה.

phrases.english: Ulla said, and some say Rav Yehuda:
Those that come after rain.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 24.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The ברייתא refers to clouds and winds that come after rain.

steps.title: But wind after rain is a curse
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: עולא himself said a curse in the תורה is about wind after rain.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does this mean that wind after rain is good? But it is written: 'ה׳ will make the rain of your land powder and dust,' and עולא, or some say רב יהודה, said: this is wind that comes after rain!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא objects: how can wind after rain be good, when the same teacher explained a curse in the תורה as being wind after rain?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The curse says rain will turn into 'powder and dust.' עולא explained that this happens when wind blows after rain and kicks up dust. So the same speaker seems to call wind after rain both a blessing and a curse.

keyTerms.meaning: Is this to say? (opens a challenge)

phrases.english: Is this to say that it is beneficial?
But isn't it written:
"The Lord will make the rain of your land
powder and dust,"
and Ulla, and some say Rav Yehuda, said:
This is wind that comes after rain!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer of step 25.
steps.kashyaTarget: עולא's explanation that clouds and winds after rain are beneficial.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: עולא also explained the curse of 'powder and dust' as wind after rain, so wind after rain cannot be a blessing.

steps.title: Gentle wind helps, strong wind harms
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers: a gentle wind after rain is good; a forceful wind after rain is the curse.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult: this one is wind that comes gently, that one is wind that comes forcefully.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא resolves the problem by splitting wind after rain into two kinds: gentle and forceful.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both of עולא's statements are true, but about different winds. A soft wind after rain is a blessing, while a strong wind dries things out and raises dust, which is the curse.

phrases.english: It is not difficult:
this is when it comes gently,
that is when it comes forcefully.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 26.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Wind after rain seemed to be one thing, both blessing and curse.
steps.terutzMaskana: Gentle wind after rain is a blessing; forceful wind after rain is the curse.

steps.title: Wind that raises dust versus wind that does not
steps.stepSummary: A second answer: wind that raises dust is the curse; wind that does not raise dust is the blessing.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say: this one raises dust, that one does not raise dust.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers another way to solve the same problem, this time based on whether the wind lifts dust.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of measuring how strong the wind is, this answer looks at the result: does it raise dust? This fits the words of the curse, 'powder and dust,' very closely.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you wish, say (introduces another answer)

phrases.english: And if you wish, say:
this is wind that raises dust,
that is wind that does not raise dust.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second answer to the same קשיא as step 27.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Wind after rain seemed to be both blessing and curse.
steps.terutzMaskana: Wind that raises dust is the curse; wind that does not raise dust is the blessing.
steps.whatToRemember: Wind after rain can be good or bad. It is good when gentle or when it does not raise dust; it is the curse of 'powder and dust' when strong or dusty.

steps.title: Wind, clouds and sun after rain
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה says wind and clouds after rain are like rain, and sun after rain is like two rains.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב יהודה said: Wind after rain is like rain. Clouds after rain are like rain. Sun after rain is like two rains.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a related teaching from רב יהודה that ranks how helpful things are after rain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Wind and clouds after rain are each worth one rainfall. Sunshine after rain is even better, worth two rainfalls, since it helps the soaked ground make things grow.

phrases.english: And Rav Yehuda said:
Wind after rain is like rain.
Clouds after rain are like rain.
Sun after rain is like two rains.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A related teaching on the same theme of what comes after rain.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Wind and clouds after rain equal one rain; sun after rain equals two rains.

steps.title: What does רב יהודה exclude?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what רב יהודה's list is meant to leave out.
steps.simpleTranslation: To exclude what?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a short question to set up the next step: if all these things are good after rain, what is not good?
steps.deeperAnalysis: By listing specific good things, רב יהודה implies that something similar is not good. The גמרא wants to know what that is.

phrases.english: To exclude what?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the limits of רב יהודה's statement in step 29.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What kind of sun or light after rain is not beneficial?

steps.title: Evening glow and patchy sun are excluded
steps.stepSummary: The excluded cases are the evening glow and sun shining through gaps between clouds.
steps.simpleTranslation: To exclude the glow of the night, and sun that shines between the clouds.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers: the glow at nightfall and sun peeking through patches of clouds are not good after rain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Only full, steady sunshine after rain is a blessing. A weak evening glow or broken sun between clouds does not count and is even harmful.

phrases.english: To exclude the glow of the night,
and sun that shines between the clouds.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 30.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Evening glow and patchy sun between clouds are excluded; they are not beneficial after rain.

steps.title: Snow on mountains is worth five rains
steps.stepSummary: רבא teaches that snow on the mountains equals five rainfalls on the land, from a פסוק in איוב.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: Snow is as good for the mountains as five rains for the land, as it says: 'For to the snow He says, be on the earth; and the shower of rain, and the showers of His mighty rain.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a related teaching from רבא about how valuable snow is, with a פסוק as the source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק links snow to rain using several rain-words. 'גשם' appears twice, 'מטר' appears once, and the plural 'מטרות' counts as two. That makes five, so snow equals five rainfalls.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not count only the separate words you see. 'גשם' appears twice and 'מטר' once, and the plural 'מטרות' counts as two. That is how the total reaches five.

phrases.english: Rava said:
Snow is beneficial to the mountains
like five rains to the land,
as it is stated:
"For to the snow He says: Fall on the earth,
and to the shower of rain,
and the showers of His mighty rain."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A related teaching on the theme of beneficial weather.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Snow on the mountains is as beneficial as five rainfalls on the land, learned from איוב 37:6.
steps.whatToRemember: After rain: wind and clouds = one rain, full sun = two rains. Snow on mountains = five rains.

steps.title: רבא matches each type of rain to what it helps
steps.stepSummary: רבא teaches that snow benefits the mountains, strong rain benefits trees, and gentle rain benefits fruit.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבא said: Snow is good for the mountains. Strong rain is good for the trees. Gentle rain is good for the fruit.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second teaching from רבא about rain. He lists different kinds of precipitation and says which part of nature each one helps most. The list continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the previous step, רבא said snow is worth five rainfalls. Now he goes further and explains that each kind of rain has its own job. Strong rain soaks deep down to tree roots, while gentle rain helps fruit grow without knocking it off or damaging it.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think strong rain is simply 'better' than gentle rain. רבא's point is that each kind of rain is best for something different.

phrases.english: And Rava said: Snow — for the mountains,
phrases.notes: The word 'and' links this teaching to רבא's previous statement about snow.

phrases.english: strong rain — for the trees,
phrases.notes: Heavy rain soaks deep enough to reach tree roots.

phrases.english: gentle rain — for the fruit,
phrases.notes: The list continues on the next amud.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second teaching of רבא on the same topic, expanding his snow statement into a full list of precipitation types and their benefits.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Each type of precipitation has a specific benefit: snow for mountains, strong rain for trees, gentle rain for fruit.
